title: Fold an outlet's three stiff copper wires back into its wall box, seat the outlet and drive its two mounting screws
instruction: Put the outlet back in its wall box with every wire inside the box, then drive its two mounting screws home with the screwdriver and let go.
context: Putting a receptacle back in its box is routine for electricians (O*NET 47-2111.00, 821,000 US jobs in 2025: "Assemble, install, test, or maintain electrical or electronic wiring, equipment, appliances, apparatus, or fixtures, using hand tools or power tools") and general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071.00, 1,621,800 jobs: "Assemble, install, or repair wiring, electrical or electronic components, pipe systems, plumbing, machinery, or equipment"). The wires are solid 12 AWG copper: they keep whatever bend they are given and push back. Pushed straight in, their loops stand up over the box's top edge and are trapped between the outlet and the wall, where a pinched conductor is a shock and fire risk. Each loop has to be folded into the box while the other hand holds the outlet, and only then will the outlet go home. The job is finished with a screwdriver: the outlet's two mounting screws are driven into the box, which pulls the strap flat onto the wall and holds it there.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table: x forward (away from the robot), y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Wall (fixed, off-white board): 32 cm wide, 30 cm tall, 1.27 cm thick, standing on the table with its front face at x 37.5, from y -24 to y +8. Wall box (fixed, blue plastic, open to the front, its rim flush with the wall's face): inside 5.2 cm wide, 9.0 cm tall and 6.6 cm deep, walls 2.5 mm thick, opening centred at y -8, 19 cm up. Inside it, on the centre line, a screw boss 1.0 cm wide stands 0.67 cm in from the top wall and another from the bottom wall; their screw holes are 8.33 cm apart. Outlet (loose, 70 g): a steel mounting strap 3.35 cm wide, 10.67 cm tall and 1.5 mm thick; an ivory plastic body 3.35 cm wide, 6.8 cm tall and 2.0 cm deep behind the strap; an ivory face 3.35 cm wide, 6.8 cm tall and 0.45 cm thick in front of it. It is not connected to power, and the strap's edges are deburred so they cannot cut the gripper pads. It hangs on its wires, upright, facing the robot, centred on the opening, with the back of its strap 11.5 cm in front of the wall. Wires (three, solid 12 AWG copper, conductor 2.05 mm across, cut fresh for every trial): one black and one white, insulated to 3.0 mm across, each 20.3 cm (8 in) long from the cable entry to its terminal, and one bare, 19.2 cm long. All three are fixed side by side at the cable entry at the top back of the box, 5.8 cm behind the wall's face, 3 cm above the opening's centre (the bare wire 2.6 cm) and 0.75 to 1.65 cm to the left of it. The black wire ends on the right side of the outlet's body and the white wire on its left side, both 1.2 cm above the outlet's centre; the bare wire ends on the left side, 3.0 cm below the centre. Each wire has two folds bent into it before it is fitted, each a V standing 9 mm off the wire's line over 32 mm of wire. On the black and the white wire: one 7.0 cm from the terminal, pointing up, and one 13.8 cm from the terminal, pointing down and to the robot's right. On the bare wire: one 7.3 cm from the terminal, pointing down, and one 13.5 cm from the terminal, pointing down and to the robot's right. Between its ends each wire runs in a shallow S, dipping below the straight line near the box's mouth and rising above it nearer the outlet. wire_start_points.csv lists each wire's path every 5 mm and wire_start_shapes.pdf is a 1:1 template of it (side and top views). Mounting screws (two zinc-plated steel 6-32 x 1 in combination pan-head device screws, heads 6.9 mm across): one captive in the slot at each end of the strap, on the outlet's centre line, 8.33 cm apart, backed out so its head rests against the front of the strap and its thread points at the wall. Screwdriver (loose, 150 g): a ratcheting #2 Phillips screwdriver set to drive, 18 cm long: a red plastic handle 11 cm long and 3.3 cm thick with two flats 2.6 cm apart, and a bare steel shaft 6 mm across and 7 cm long, ending in the point. It lies on a rest with its axis 12 cm above the table, the middle of its handle at x 40, y 30, pointing away from the robot, flats upright. Rest (fixed, grey plastic): a base plate 13 cm long, 6 cm wide and 0.4 cm thick, centred under the middle of the handle, with two posts, each 1.2 cm thick along the screwdriver: one 2.0 cm wide under the back end of the handle (at x 35.7), its top 10.5 cm above the table, and one 2.8 cm wide under the front end (at x 43.1), its top 10.6 cm above the table. A cheek 0.4 cm thick stands on each side of the front post, 1.2 cm higher than it, and the two keep the flats upright. The 6 cm of the handle between the posts is clear for the gripper. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured on the last step from the outlet's pose, 20 or 21 points along each wire, the two screws' positions, and the positions of the grippers and the screwdriver's tip. Score 0 unless all of these hold: the outlet is upright (its long axis within 15 degrees of vertical); every corner of its strap is within 15 mm of the wall's face (near enough for a 1 in mounting screw to reach its hole); every wire is inside the box (no point of a wire more than 2 mm in front of the wall's face, apart from the last 5 mm at the outlet's terminal, which is part of the outlet; and no point outside the opening's outline within 3 mm of the face); and the outlet has been let go (the grip centre and pad tips of both grippers and the screwdriver's tip at least 3 cm from the outlet and from every wire, with the outlet at rest (no corner of its strap moving more than 1 mm), for the last 2 s). Then: 0.25 if either of the strap's screw slots is more than 3 mm from its screw hole in the box, measured across the wall; 0.5 if both are on their holes and no screw is driven home; 0.75 with one screw home; 1.0 with both. A screw is home when it is threaded into its hole and its head is down on the strap with that end of the strap on the wall (no more than 1 mm between the head's underside and the strap's front). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Doing nothing, a push that leaves a wire trapped or showing, and an outlet still held or pressed in place all score 0. On a real rig the strap's corners and the screw holes are measured with a ruler, a screw is home when a 1 mm feeler will not go under its head and the strap does not lift off the wall there, and the wire rule is read from three photos taken once the grippers are away: one square-on from the front, and one along the wall's face from each side, level with the opening's centre, with a strip 2 mm thick stuck to the wall 3 cm below the opening as the reference. A wire fails if, anywhere other than the last 5 mm at its terminal, more than half its thickness stands further from the wall than the strip's face in a side photo, or if any part of it lies on the wall or the box's rim outside the opening in any photo. A scoring outlet is within 15 mm of the wall and its body is as wide as its strap, so the two side photos between them show all of the space in front of the wall, behind the strap included. Any part of a wire that no photo shows is therefore behind the wall's face, inside the box, which is where the rule wants it: wire hidden behind the outlet cannot break the rule unseen.
reset_notes: Every trial starts with fresh wire, so the starting shape and stiffness are the same each time. Cut three new lengths from the same reels (free lengths 20.3, 20.3 and 19.2 cm, plus what the entry clamp and the terminal screw take). Mark each fold's place from the terminal end and bend it once on a three-pin block (two 6 mm pins 32 mm apart and a third midway) until the V stands 9 mm off the wire's line, within 1 mm. Fit each wire to its terminal and the cable entry with its folds pointing as the setup lists, pull the outlet out until the back of its strap is 11.5 cm in front of the wall, and shape each wire by hand against the 1:1 template (wire_start_shapes.pdf) until it follows it to within 3 mm. About 5 minutes. Used wires are thrown away, never straightened and used again: copper work-hardens where it is bent, so only new wire bent once the same way starts with the same stiffness. In the simulator every reset restores this shape and each fold's starting hardening, with nothing carried over from the last trial. Back both mounting screws out of the box until their heads rest against the strap, and put the screwdriver back on its rest, set to drive.
fidelity: Wires: chains of rigid 10.7 mm links on two-axis joints that bend like solid 12 AWG copper (E 117 GPa, first yield 59 N mm, work hardening from annealed copper's curve), so a bend stays and stiffens; no twist or stretch. Screws: our model, not simulated threads. The bit drives a screw while its tip is on the head within 2 mm of the axis; forward turns count, back turns slip (the ratchet); 2 turns take a screw home (really about 30); no torque is needed. Outlet, box and wall: rigid, true size.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 after 4,800 steps (termination: step limit); scripted demo: 1.0 after 2,971 steps (termination: success)
